meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of house prices on floor area and number of rooms finds that each regressor is highly significant on its own, but when both are included, both standard errors are large and both t-statistics are small. Floor area and rooms have a correlation of 0.95. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The two regressors move together, so the data say little about either one holding the other fixed.
options.feedback: Correct. With so little independent variation, each coefficient is imprecisely estimated, so its standard error is large.

options.text: Rooms must be what really drives price, so floor area should be dropped from the model.
options.feedback: Nothing in the standard errors says which variable 'really' matters; collinearity only makes it hard to separate the two.

options.text: Including both regressors made the errors heteroskedastic, which inflated the standard errors.
options.feedback: The inflation comes from the regressors' correlation with each other (the VIF), not from the error variance.

options.text: The OLS coefficients have become biased, which is why both of the t-statistics fell so sharply.
options.feedback: Multicollinearity leaves OLS unbiased; it lowers precision, which is what inflates the standard errors.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.1: when regressors are highly correlated, OLS stays unbiased, but individual coefficients are imprecise: standard errors rise and t-statistics fall, even when the variables matter jointly.

practice.stem: Suppose regressing x₃ on the other regressors of a model gives an auxiliary R² of 0.95. What is the VIF for x₃?

options.text: About 1.05
options.feedback: This is 1/0.95. The VIF divides 1 by (1 − R²), the share of x₃'s variation the other regressors do not explain.

options.text: About 4.5
options.feedback: This is √20, the factor by which the standard error is inflated. The VIF itself inflates the variance.

options.text: About 10.3
options.feedback: This squares R² first: 1/(1 − 0.95²). The formula uses the auxiliary R² as it is.

options.text: About 20
options.feedback: Correct: VIF = 1/(1 − 0.95) = 1/0.05 = 20, well above the chapter's threshold of 10.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.1: VIF<sub>j</sub> = 1/(1 − R<sub>j</sub>²), where R<sub>j</sub>² comes from regressing x<sub>j</sub> on all other regressors. R² = 0.95 gives VIF = 20.

practice.stem: Suppose a regressor has a VIF of exactly 1. Then the other regressors explain none of its variation, and its standard error is not inflated by multicollinearity.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. VIF = 1 means R<sub>j</sub>² = 0: the regressor is uncorrelated with the others, so there is no inflation.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Solve VIF = 1/(1 − R<sub>j</sub>²) = 1 for R<sub>j</sub>²: it gives R<sub>j</sub>² = 0, the no-collinearity case.

practice.explanation: Section 16.1: VIF = 1 is the ideal case (no multicollinearity). VIF = 5 corresponds to R<sub>j</sub>² = 0.80 and VIF = 10 to R<sub>j</sub>² = 0.90.

practice.concept: Variance inflation factor and standard errors (Section 16.1, Key Concept 16.1)
practice.stem: Suppose a regressor has a VIF of 9. Compared with a situation with no collinearity, by about what factor is its standard error inflated?

options.text: About 81
options.feedback: This squares the VIF. The VIF already measures the inflation of the variance, and the standard error is its square root.

options.text: About 9
options.feedback: 9 is the inflation of the variance. The standard error is the square root of the variance.

options.text: About 0.89
options.feedback: This is the auxiliary R² (1 − 1/9), not an inflation factor.

options.text: About 3
options.feedback: Correct: the standard error is inflated by √VIF = √9 = 3.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.1: the VIF inflates the variance of b<sub>j</sub>, so the standard error is inflated by √VIF. The chapter's example: VIF = 10 inflates the standard error by √10 ≈ 3.2.

practice.stem: Suppose you want to know whether income and wealth matter for household saving, but the two are highly correlated (both VIFs are above 20). Which approach does the chapter recommend?

options.text: Judge each variable by its own t-test, keeping only those with |t| above 2.
options.feedback: Individual t-tests are unreliable under multicollinearity: inflated standard errors make each variable look insignificant.

options.text: Test the hypothesis that both coefficients are zero with a joint F-test.
options.feedback: Correct. The joint test evaluates the combined contribution, which collinearity does not blur.

options.text: Switch to heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, which remove the collinearity.
options.feedback: Robust SEs address nonconstant error variance; they do nothing about correlation among regressors.

options.text: Drop whichever variable has the smaller t-statistic, then test the other one alone.
options.feedback: Dropping a variable is an option only if the research question does not need it; a small t-statistic under collinearity is not a reason by itself.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.2: under multicollinearity, individual t-tests are unreliable, but joint F-tests remain powerful. Test groups of correlated regressors together.

practice.stem: Suppose you add a regressor that is highly collinear with one already in the model, and the standard errors of both rise sharply. Then the model's overall R² will fall.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Adding a regressor never lowers the OLS R²; collinearity shows up in the standard errors of individual coefficients instead.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Adding a regressor can never lower the OLS R², however collinear the new regressor is.

practice.explanation: Section 16.1: adding a regressor can never lower the OLS R². What multicollinearity damages is the precision of individual coefficients: their standard errors rise and their t-statistics fall.

practice.concept: Consequences of OLS assumption violations (Sections 16.2–16.4, Key Concept 16.3)
practice.stem: In which of these situations would the OLS slope estimates be biased? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In a cross-section of firms, the error variance is larger for big firms than for small ones.
options.feedback: This is heteroskedasticity: OLS stays unbiased; only the default standard errors are wrong.

options.text: In a wage regression, unmeasured ability raises wages and is correlated with education.
options.feedback: Correct. An omitted variable correlated with a regressor makes the regressor endogenous: OLS is biased.

options.text: In a market regression, price affects quantity and quantity also affects price.
options.feedback: Correct. Simultaneous causality makes the regressor correlated with the error, which biases OLS.

options.text: In a quarterly sales regression, a shock in one quarter carries over into the next quarter.
options.feedback: This is autocorrelation: OLS stays unbiased, but default standard errors are wrong.

options.text: The regressor of interest is recorded with large random measurement error.
options.feedback: Correct. The chapter lists measurement error among the causes of endogeneity, which biases OLS.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.3: an incorrect model or endogeneity makes OLS biased and inconsistent. Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation leave OLS unbiased but make the default standard errors wrong.

practice.stem: Suppose a city-level regression of crime on police officers per capita suffers from reverse causality: police reduce crime, but cities with more crime also hire more police. What does this imply for the OLS coefficient on police?

options.text: It is unbiased, but its default standard error is too small, so heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors solve the problem.
options.feedback: Robust standard errors fix the standard errors only; they cannot remove a bias in the coefficient itself.

options.text: Its bias shrinks to zero as more cities are added, so the remedy is a larger sample.
options.feedback: Endogeneity makes OLS inconsistent: the bias does not disappear as the sample grows.

options.text: OLS is inconsistent: police per capita moves with the error, so the estimate is biased even in large samples.
options.feedback: Correct. Reverse causality violates the zero-conditional-mean assumption; the chapter's remedy is an instrumental variable.

options.text: It is unbiased but imprecise, just as with highly correlated regressors.
options.feedback: Multicollinearity costs precision only; reverse causality biases the coefficient.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.3 and the glossary: a regressor correlated with the error (endogeneity) biases OLS, and neither robust standard errors nor more data fix it. Instrumental variables are the standard remedy.

practice.stem: Suppose a researcher uses each person's distance to the nearest college as an instrument for years of schooling in a wage regression. What must be true for distance to be a valid instrument?

options.text: Distance must shift years of schooling and affect wages only through schooling.
options.feedback: Correct: relevance (it moves schooling) and exogeneity (no direct path to wages).

options.text: Distance must be strongly correlated with wages and unrelated to schooling.
options.feedback: An instrument must move the endogenous regressor (schooling); a direct link to wages would violate exogeneity.

options.text: Distance must be unrelated to both schooling and wages, so that it adds no bias.
options.feedback: An instrument unrelated to schooling cannot isolate any variation in it: relevance fails.

options.text: Distance must be correlated with the error term, so that it captures the omitted factors.
options.feedback: A valid instrument is uncorrelated with the error; that is what lets it isolate the exogenous part of schooling.

practice.explanation: Glossary (Instrumental Variable): z must (i) shift the endogenous regressor x and (ii) affect y only through x. Two-stage least squares then uses the part of x that z explains.

practice.concept: Sources of endogeneity (Sections 16.2–16.4, Key Concepts glossary)
practice.stem: In a city-level regression of crime on police per capita, which of these would make police per capita endogenous? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Cities with more crime respond by hiring more police.
options.feedback: Correct: simultaneous (reverse) causality correlates the regressor with the error.

options.text: Unobserved local economic conditions affect both crime and police budgets.
options.feedback: Correct: an omitted variable that drives both the outcome and the regressor ends up in the error.

options.text: Police per capita is highly correlated with the city's population density, which is also in the model.
options.feedback: Correlation among regressors is multicollinearity: it costs precision but does not correlate the regressor with the error.

options.text: Police per capita is recorded with large random errors in many cities.
options.feedback: Correct: the glossary lists measurement error in the regressor as a source of endogeneity.

practice.explanation: Glossary (Endogeneity): a regressor is endogenous when it is correlated with the error, typically because of an omitted variable, simultaneous causality, or measurement error.

practice.concept: Omitted variables bias formula (Key Takeaways, Practice Exercise 1)
practice.stem: Suppose a wage regression omits ability. Ability raises wages (β₃ > 0) and is positively correlated with education (δ₂₃ > 0). Using Bias = β₃ × δ₂₃, how is the education coefficient affected?

options.text: It is biased upward: it overstates the effect of education.
options.feedback: Correct: a positive β₃ times a positive δ₂₃ gives a positive bias.

options.text: It is biased downward: it understates the effect of education.
options.feedback: Multiply the signs: (+) × (+) is positive, so the estimate is pushed up, not down.

options.text: It is unbiased, because ability is not in the model.
options.feedback: Leaving out a relevant variable that is correlated with an included regressor is exactly what creates the bias.

options.text: Its bias cannot be signed without knowing the standard errors.
options.feedback: The sign of the bias depends only on the signs of β₃ and δ₂₃, not on standard errors.

practice.explanation: Key Takeaways: Bias = β₃ × δ₂₃, where β₃ is the omitted variable's effect and δ₂₃ the slope from regressing the omitted variable on the included regressor. (+) × (+) means upward bias.

practice.stem: Suppose a coefficient is 2.40, with a default standard error of 0.80 and a heteroskedasticity-robust standard error of 1.20. What is the t-statistic based on the robust standard error?

options.feedback: This uses the default standard error (2.40/0.80). The robust t-statistic divides by the robust standard error.
This multiplies the default t (3.0) by the ratio of standard errors (1.5). A larger standard error lowers t.
Correct: t = 2.40/1.20 = 2.0. The coefficient is unchanged; only the standard error moves.
This divides the standard error by the coefficient (1.20/2.40). t is the coefficient divided by its standard error.

practice.explanation: Section 16.5: robust standard errors leave the coefficient unchanged; t = coefficient ÷ robust SE = 2.40/1.20 = 2.0, down from 3.0 with the default SE.

practice.concept: Comparing default and robust standard errors (Section 16.5)
practice.stem: Suppose that in a regression the robust standard error of one coefficient is slightly smaller than its default standard error (ratio 0.97). This shows that the robust standard errors were computed incorrectly.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Robust SEs are usually, not always, larger than default SEs; a ratio slightly below 1 can occur for some coefficients (Section 16.5).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Robust SEs are often larger, but the ratio can fall slightly below 1 for some coefficients.

practice.explanation: Section 16.5: robust SEs are usually larger (more conservative), but not always. A ratio near 1 suggests little heteroskedasticity affecting that coefficient.

practice.stem: Suppose a cross-sectional regression of wages on education and experience for 5,000 workers is re-estimated with HC1 (White) standard errors instead of default ones. What changes?

options.text: The coefficients change, because HC1 gives less weight to workers with large residuals.
options.feedback: HC1 does not reweight observations; the OLS coefficients are identical under both kinds of standard errors.

options.text: The R² changes, because the robust model explains a different share of the variation in wages.
options.feedback: R² depends on the fitted values and residuals, which HC1 leaves untouched.

options.text: Nothing changes in a large sample, because robust standard errors matter only in small samples.
options.feedback: The chapter recommends robust SEs for cross-sections of any size; they are asymptotically valid, so large samples are where they work best.

options.text: The coefficients stay the same, while the standard errors, t-statistics, and confidence intervals can change.
options.feedback: Correct. HC1 changes only the measure of uncertainty, not the estimates.

practice.explanation: Section 16.5: with HC1 standard errors, coefficient estimates are unchanged and only standard errors (and everything built from them) are adjusted.

practice.stem: Suppose the residuals from a monthly time-series regression have a lag-1 autocorrelation of −0.5. What does this mean?

options.text: Half of the residuals in the sample are negative and half are positive.
options.feedback: Autocorrelation is a correlation between residuals and their own past values, not a share of negative residuals.

options.text: A positive residual tends to be followed by a negative one, and a negative by a positive.
options.feedback: Correct. A negative lag-1 autocorrelation means consecutive residuals tend to switch sign.

options.text: The residuals shrink by half in absolute size from one month to the next one.
options.feedback: Autocorrelation describes how residuals co-move with their past values, not a steady decline in their size.

options.text: There is no autocorrelation at all, since only positive values count as dependence.
options.feedback: Negative autocorrelation is also dependence over time; it violates the independence assumption too.

practice.explanation: Section 16.6: with uₜ = ρuₜ₋₁ + εₜ, the lag-1 autocorrelation is ρ. With ρ = −0.5, a residual of +1 is followed on average by −0.5.

practice.stem: Suppose the residual ACF of a quarterly regression shows autocorrelations of 0.6, 0.36, and 0.22 at lags 1–3, all well outside the confidence band, and decaying steadily after that. This pattern is a classic signature of AR(1) errors.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. AR(1) errors with ρ = 0.6 have autocorrelations ρ, ρ², ρ³, … = 0.6, 0.36, 0.22: geometric decay.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Compare the values with 0.6, 0.6², and 0.6³: geometric decay is what AR(1) errors produce (Section 16.6).

practice.explanation: Section 16.6: an AR(1) error process produces autocorrelations that decay geometrically (ρ, ρ², ρ³, …); bars outside the band signal significant autocorrelation.

practice.stem: Suppose a time series has n = 300 observations and AR(1) errors with ρ = 0.5. Using the chapter's variance factor (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ), what is the approximate effective sample size?

options.text: About 150
options.feedback: This multiplies n by (1 − ρ). The effective sample size divides n by the variance factor (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ) = 3.

options.text: About 100
options.feedback: Correct: the factor is 1.5/0.5 = 3, so the effective sample size is about 300/3 = 100.

options.text: About 900
options.feedback: This multiplies n by the factor. Autocorrelation reduces the information in the sample, so n is divided by it.

options.text: About 173
options.feedback: This divides n by √3. The factor (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ) applies to the variance, so n is divided by the factor itself.

practice.explanation: Section 16.6: with AR(1) errors, Var(ū) ≈ σ²·(1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ)·(1/n), so the effective sample size is about n divided by (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ): 300/3 = 100.

practice.stem: Suppose a quarterly regression of GDP growth on interest rates has strongly positively autocorrelated errors. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Default t-statistics tend to overstate the evidence against the null.
options.feedback: Correct. Default standard errors are typically too small, so t-statistics are too large.

options.text: The OLS coefficient on interest rates is biased by the autocorrelation.
options.feedback: Autocorrelation leaves OLS unbiased and consistent; the problem is the standard errors.

options.text: HAC (Newey–West) standard errors give valid inference.
options.feedback: Correct. HAC standard errors are the chapter's remedy for autocorrelated errors.

options.text: The fix is to drop the regressor with the largest t-statistic.
options.feedback: Autocorrelation calls for a different inference method, not a different set of regressors.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.5: with autocorrelated errors, OLS is unbiased, but default SEs are typically too small, overstating significance. HAC (Newey–West) SEs give valid inference.

practice.stem: Suppose a time series has T = 1,000 observations. What lag length L does the chapter's rule of thumb L ≈ 0.75 × T<sup>1/3</sup> give?

options.text: About 7.5
options.feedback: Correct: the cube root of 1,000 is 10, and 0.75 × 10 = 7.5, so about 7 or 8 lags.

options.text: About 24
options.feedback: This uses the square root of T (0.75 × √1,000). The rule uses the cube root.

options.text: About 750
options.feedback: This multiplies 0.75 by T itself. The rule uses the cube root of T, which grows slowly.

options.text: About 10
options.feedback: This is the cube root of T alone; the rule multiplies it by 0.75.

practice.concept: Omitted variables bias in practice (Section 16.7, Key Concept 16.6)
practice.stem: Suppose the coefficient on education in a wage regression falls from 0.10 to 0.07 when a test score measuring ability is added as a control. By what percentage did the education coefficient fall?

options.text: About 3%
options.feedback: 0.03 is the fall in the coefficient itself (0.10 − 0.07), not a percentage of the original value.

options.text: About 43%
options.feedback: This divides the fall by the new value (0.03/0.07). A percentage change divides by the starting value, 0.10.

options.text: About 30%
options.feedback: Correct: (0.10 − 0.07)/0.10 = 0.30, a 30% fall once ability is controlled for.

options.text: About 70%
options.feedback: This is the new value as a share of the old (0.07/0.10); the fall is the rest.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.6: (0.10 − 0.07)/0.10 = 30%. Controlling for ability changes the education estimate: omitted variables bias.

practice.stem: Suppose a residual-versus-fitted plot shows a roughly constant spread, but the LOWESS smooth is U-shaped: residuals are positive at low and high fitted values and negative in the middle. What does this suggest?

options.text: Heteroskedasticity, so robust standard errors are needed for inference.
options.feedback: Heteroskedasticity concerns how the spread of the residuals changes, and the spread here is constant.

options.text: Autocorrelation, so HAC standard errors are needed.
options.feedback: Autocorrelation is a time-series pattern (runs of same-sign residuals over time), not visible in a residual-versus-fitted scatter.

options.text: Multicollinearity, so VIFs should be computed.
options.feedback: Multicollinearity concerns the regressors' correlation with each other; it does not curve the residual pattern.

options.text: A missing nonlinear term, so try a quadratic or a transformation.
options.feedback: Correct. A curved LOWESS means the residuals vary systematically with the fitted values: the functional form is wrong.

practice.explanation: Section 16.8: in a residual-versus-fitted plot, a curved LOWESS means the residuals vary systematically with the fitted values: add polynomial terms or transform the variables.

practice.stem: Which statements about the chapter's diagnostic plots are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A component-plus-residual plot for x<sub>j</sub> graphs b<sub>j</sub>x<sub>j</sub> + e against x<sub>j</sub>.
options.feedback: Correct. Adding back the regressor's estimated component shows its partial relationship with y.

options.text: In a well-specified model, residuals scatter randomly around zero with constant spread.
options.feedback: Correct. That is the benchmark against which the plots are judged.

options.text: An added-variable plot purges both y and x<sub>j</sub> of the other regressors before plotting them.
options.feedback: Correct. It shows the partial relationship of y and x<sub>j</sub>.

options.text: Residual-versus-regressor plots are needed only for regressors whose coefficients are statistically significant.
options.feedback: The plots check every regressor's functional form and spread, whatever its t-statistic.

options.text: Residual-versus-regressor plots examine one regressor at a time, looking for curvature or a changing spread linked to it.
options.feedback: Correct. They check for nonlinearity or heteroskedasticity related to that regressor.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.7: residual-versus-regressor, component-plus-residual, and added-variable plots each examine one regressor; residuals of a well-specified model scatter randomly around zero with constant spread.

practice.stem: Suppose a wage regression includes experience, and you want to check whether wages rise linearly with experience after accounting for the model. What does a component-plus-residual plot for experience show?

options.text: Wages plotted against experience, ignoring all of the other regressors in the model.
options.feedback: That is a raw scatter plot; it mixes in the effects of the other regressors.

options.text: Residuals plotted against fitted wages, to check whether the spread of the errors is constant.
options.feedback: That is the residual-versus-fitted plot, which looks at the model as a whole.

options.text: The VIF of experience plotted against the R² of its auxiliary regression on the others.
options.feedback: VIFs diagnose multicollinearity; they are not part of the component-plus-residual plot.

options.text: The experience component of the fit plus the residual, plotted against experience.
options.feedback: Correct: b<sub>exp</sub> × experience + e versus experience, which shows the partial relationship with experience.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.7: the component-plus-residual plot graphs b<sub>j</sub>x<sub>j</sub> + e against x<sub>j</sub>, showing the partial relationship between y and that regressor.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression has k = 5 coefficients (including the intercept) and n = 100 observations. Using the chapter's rule of thumb, above what absolute value of DFITS should an observation be investigated?

options.feedback: This is √(k/n) without the factor of 2: the rule is 2√(k/n).
This is 2/√n, the chapter's threshold for DFBETAS, not DFITS.
This is 2k/n, without the square root. The DFITS rule is 2√(k/n).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.8: investigate if |DFITS<sub>i</sub>| > 2√(k/n). With k = 5 and n = 100: 2√0.05 ≈ 0.45.

practice.stem: Suppose that in a regression with n = 100, one firm has a DFBETAS of 0.35 for the coefficient on advertising, while its DFBETAS values for the other coefficients are all near zero. What does this indicate?

options.text: The firm's own fitted value changes a lot when it is dropped, but no coefficient does.
options.feedback: That describes DFITS. DFBETAS measures the change in individual coefficients.

options.text: The firm is a data error and must be deleted.
options.feedback: A flag calls for investigation; it does not prove an error, and the chapter warns against automatic deletion.

options.text: Dropping the firm would noticeably move the advertising coefficient but barely move the others.
options.feedback: Correct. 0.35 exceeds the threshold 2/√100 = 0.20, and DFBETAS is coefficient-specific: this firm is influential for the advertising coefficient only.

options.text: The firm has high leverage but no influence on any coefficient.
options.feedback: A DFBETAS above the threshold is direct evidence of influence on that coefficient.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 16.8: DFBETAS<sub>j,i</sub> is the scaled change in b<sub>j</sub> when observation i is dropped; investigate if it exceeds 2/√n (0.20 here). One observation can matter for one coefficient and not for others.

practice.stem: Suppose 4 of 100 observations exceed the DFITS threshold, and checking the original source shows that one of them was mistyped (an extra zero). Correcting that value and re-estimating follows the chapter's advice.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The first step is to investigate the data; if a value is an error, correct or remove it.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the steps the chapter lists for handling influential observations (Section 16.8).

practice.explanation: Section 16.8: the first step with a flagged observation is to check the data; a value that turns out to be a data error is corrected (or removed).

practice.concept: Leverage and influence (Section 16.8, Key Concepts glossary)
practice.stem: Suppose one observation has perfectly ordinary regressor values (near the center of the data) but a very large residual. What does this mean?

options.text: It is an outlier in y, but its low leverage limits how much it can pull the fitted line.
options.feedback: Correct. Influence combines leverage and residual size; a point near the center of x has little leverage.

options.text: It has high leverage, because an observation's leverage depends on the size of its residual.
options.feedback: Leverage depends only on how unusual the regressor values are, not on y or the residual.

options.text: It must be the most influential observation in the sample.
options.feedback: A large residual alone does not make a point the most influential; leverage matters too.

options.text: It cannot affect any of the influence diagnostics, since its regressor values are typical.
options.feedback: A large residual can still raise its DFITS and Cook's distance somewhat, and it will stand out in residual plots.

practice.explanation: Glossary (Leverage, Cook's Distance): leverage measures how unusual xᵢ is; influence measures like Cook's distance combine leverage with residual size.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression has n = 200 observations. Using the glossary's rule of thumb for Cook's distance, above what value should an observation be investigated?

options.feedback: This is 2/n. The glossary's rule for Cook's distance is 4/n.
This is 4/√n. The rule for Cook's distance divides by n itself.
This is 1/n. The rule uses 4/n.

practice.explanation: Glossary (Cook's Distance): investigate any observation with Cook's D above 4/n; here 4/200 = 0.02.

practice.stem: Suppose Ramsey's RESET test (which adds ŷ² and ŷ³ to the regression) rejects at the 1% level. This shows that the errors are heteroskedastic, so switching to robust standard errors fixes the problem.

options.text: True
options.feedback: RESET tests the functional form: rejection signals a misspecified model (typically a missing nonlinear term), which robust SEs cannot fix.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. RESET rejection points to a misspecified functional form; the fix is a more flexible model.

practice.explanation: Glossary (RESET): adding powers of the fitted values and testing them jointly checks the functional form. Rejection calls for nonlinear terms, not different standard errors.

practice.concept: Choosing remedies for data and model problems (Sections 16.1–16.8)
practice.stem: Which of these responses to a diagnosed problem follow the chapter's guidance? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Persistent shocks in a quarterly time-series regression: HAC (Newey–West) standard errors
options.feedback: Correct: autocorrelated errors call for HAC standard errors.

options.text: A suspected missing nonlinear term: add a quadratic and check whether the curvature in the residual plot disappears
options.feedback: Correct: curvature signals a misspecified functional form, which calls for polynomial terms or transformations.

options.text: An endogenous regressor: collect a much larger sample so that the bias averages out
options.feedback: Endogeneity bias does not shrink with more data; it calls for instrumental variables or a better specification.

options.text: Two highly collinear regressors when the research question needs only one of them: drop the other
options.feedback: Correct: dropping a collinear variable is acceptable when the question does not require both.

options.text: Heteroskedastic errors: delete the observations with the largest residuals before re-estimating
options.feedback: Heteroskedasticity calls for robust standard errors (or WLS), not deleting data.

practice.explanation: Sections 16.1–16.8: match the remedy to the problem: HAC for autocorrelation, nonlinear terms for a wrong functional form, IV or better specification for endogeneity, and dropping a redundant variable (when the question allows) for multicollinearity. Deleting data is not a remedy for heteroskedasticity.

exam.stem: In the earnings data (872 workers), adding agebyeduc (age × education) to the regression of earnings on age and education raises the robust standard error of age from 151 to 719, and age's coefficient moves from 525 to 127. Which explanation fits the chapter?

options.text: Age turns out to be unrelated to earnings once education is held constant.
options.feedback: Revisit what individual standard errors and t-statistics can and cannot show when regressors overlap (Section 16.1).

options.text: Agebyeduc is largely predictable from age and education, so the data cannot separate their effects.
options.feedback: Correct. The three regressors share most of their variation, so each separate coefficient is imprecise.

options.text: The interaction term made the errors heteroskedastic, which in turn inflated the standard error of age.
options.feedback: Revisit where the inflation in this standard error comes from (Section 16.1, Key Concept 16.1).

options.text: Adding the interaction biased the age coefficient toward zero, which is why it fell from 525 to 127.
options.feedback: Revisit how the age estimates change when the interaction is added (Section 16.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.1: the interaction is nearly a linear combination of age and education, so the standard errors of the individual coefficients balloon. The problem is precision: the data cannot separate the effects.

exam.concept: Auxiliary regression and the VIF (Section 16.1, Key Concept 16.1)
exam.stem: The chapter's auxiliary regression of agebyeduc on age and education has R² = 0.973. What is the variance inflation factor for agebyeduc?

options.text: About 1.03
options.feedback: Revisit how the VIF is computed from the auxiliary R² (Key Concept 16.1).

options.text: About 6.1
options.feedback: Revisit how the VIF is computed from the auxiliary R² (Key Concept 16.1).

options.text: About 37
About 19
options.feedback: Revisit how the VIF is computed from the auxiliary R² (Key Concept 16.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.1: VIF<sub>j</sub> = 1/(1 − R<sub>j</sub>²) = 1/(1 − 0.973) ≈ 37 (the exact R² gives 36.9), far above the chapter's threshold of 10 for serious multicollinearity.

exam.stem: In the earnings data, centering age and education (each minus its mean) before forming their interaction is one of the chapter's remedies for the high VIFs, because it reduces the correlation between the main effects and the interaction.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Centering reduces the correlation between the main effects and the interaction; in these data the VIFs fall from 22.0, 17.3, and 36.9 to about 1.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's list of solutions for multicollinearity created by an interaction term (Section 16.1).

exam.explanation: Section 16.1: centering before forming an interaction reduces the correlation between the main effects and the interaction. In these data, the VIFs fall from 22.0 (age), 17.3 (education), and 36.9 (agebyeduc) to about 1.

exam.concept: Variance inflation factor and standard errors (Section 16.1, Key Concept 16.1)
exam.stem: In the interaction model, education has a VIF of 17.3. Compared with a situation in which education were uncorrelated with the other regressors, by about what factor is its standard error inflated?

options.text: About 17.3
options.feedback: Revisit how the VIF relates to the variance and to the standard error (Key Concept 16.1).

options.text: About 299
options.feedback: Revisit how the VIF relates to the variance and to the standard error (Key Concept 16.1).

options.text: About 4.2
options.feedback: Correct: the standard error is inflated by √17.3 ≈ 4.2.

options.text: About 0.94
options.feedback: Revisit how the VIF relates to the variance and to the standard error (Key Concept 16.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.1: the VIF inflates the variance of b<sub>j</sub>, so the standard error is inflated by √VIF = √17.3 ≈ 4.2.

exam.stem: In the model earnings ~ age + education + agebyeduc (robust SEs), age has t = 0.18 (p = 0.86) and agebyeduc has t = 0.52 (p = 0.60). The joint test of H₀: both coefficients equal zero gives p ≈ 0.002. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: Age matters for earnings, but its main effect and its interaction effect are each imprecisely estimated.
options.feedback: Correct. The joint test detects the combined contribution that the individual t-tests cannot isolate.

options.text: Age has no effect on earnings, since neither of its two coefficients is statistically significant on its own.
options.feedback: Revisit what individual t-tests can show when regressors are highly correlated (Key Concept 16.2).

options.text: The joint test must be in error, since its conclusion contradicts both of the individual t-tests.
options.feedback: Revisit what a joint test evaluates compared with individual t-tests (Key Concept 16.2).

options.text: Agebyeduc should be dropped from the model, since a p-value of 0.60 shows it is unrelated to earnings.
options.feedback: Revisit what individual t-tests can show when regressors are highly correlated (Key Concept 16.2).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.2: under multicollinearity, individual t-tests are unreliable, but joint tests remain powerful. Here age and agebyeduc are jointly significant (p ≈ 0.002), so age matters even though neither coefficient is significant alone.

exam.stem: The interaction model's R² (0.1153) is essentially the same as the base model's (0.1150). By the chapter's account, the interaction model's high VIFs do not make its predictions of earnings unreliable.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Multicollinearity damages the precision of individual coefficients, not the fitted values.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's list of what multicollinearity does and does not affect (Section 16.1).

exam.explanation: Section 16.1: despite high VIFs, OLS remains unbiased, predictions remain accurate, joint tests remain powerful, and the overall R² is essentially unchanged; what breaks is the interpretation of individual coefficients.

exam.concept: Consequences of OLS assumption violations (Sections 16.2–16.4, Key Concept 16.3)
exam.stem: Using the chapter's classification of assumption violations, in which situations would the OLS slope estimates remain unbiased (even if inference needs fixing)? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In an earnings regression, the error variance is larger for highly educated workers.
options.feedback: Correct. This is heteroskedasticity: coefficients stay unbiased; the standard errors need fixing.

options.text: Growth raises democracy, and democracy also raises growth.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's table of assumption violations and their consequences (Key Concept 16.3).

options.text: A needed quadratic term in age is left out of an earnings regression.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's table of assumption violations and their consequences (Key Concept 16.3).

options.text: In a quarterly time series, shocks persist from one quarter into the next.
options.feedback: Correct. This is autocorrelation: coefficients stay unbiased; the standard errors need fixing.

options.text: A variable that affects democracy and is correlated with growth is omitted from the democracy regression.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's table of assumption violations and their consequences (Key Concept 16.3).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.3: an incorrect model or endogeneity makes OLS biased and inconsistent. Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation leave OLS unbiased but make default standard errors wrong.

exam.concept: Two-way causality and the OLS estimate (Sections 16.2–16.4)
exam.stem: In the regression of democracy on growth (131 countries), suppose that democratization itself raises growth, so causality runs in both directions. What does this imply for the OLS coefficient on growth?

options.text: It is unbiased, because OLS is unbiased whenever the errors are homoskedastic and uncorrelated.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's table of assumption violations and their consequences (Key Concept 16.3).

options.text: It is biased in small samples, but with 131 countries the bias is negligible.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's table of assumption violations and their consequences (Key Concept 16.3).

options.text: It is unbiased, because reverse causality affects only the R², not the slope.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's table of assumption violations and their consequences (Key Concept 16.3).

options.text: It is biased and inconsistent, because growth is correlated with the error term.
options.feedback: Correct. Simultaneous causality makes growth endogenous, violating E[u | x] = 0.

exam.explanation: Glossary (Endogeneity) and Key Concept 16.3: when a regressor is correlated with the error, as with simultaneous causality, OLS is biased and inconsistent; neither robust standard errors nor more data fix it. The remedy is an instrumental variable.

exam.stem: Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson (2001) use historical settler mortality as an instrument for the quality of a country's institutions. Which pair of properties must settler mortality have for this to be a valid instrument?

options.text: It must predict modern income well on its own, whether or not it is related to institutions.
options.feedback: Revisit the two conditions in the glossary entry on instrumental variables.

options.text: It must be correlated with institutions; whether it also affects income through other channels does not matter.
options.feedback: Revisit the two conditions in the glossary entry on instrumental variables.

options.text: It must be unrelated to institutions, so that it is not contaminated by the endogeneity.
options.feedback: Revisit the two conditions in the glossary entry on instrumental variables.

options.text: It must shift institutions and affect modern income only through institutions.
options.feedback: Correct: relevance (it moves institutions) and exogeneity (no direct path to the outcome).

exam.explanation: Glossary (Instrumental Variable): a valid instrument z (i) shifts the endogenous regressor and (ii) affects the outcome only through it. Two-stage least squares then uses the variation in institutions that settler mortality explains.

exam.concept: Sources of endogeneity (Sections 16.2–16.4, Key Concepts glossary)
exam.stem: In the regression of democracy on growth, which of these, if true, would make growth endogenous? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Growth is highly correlated with another regressor in the model, such as indcent (year of independence).
options.feedback: Revisit the glossary entry on endogeneity and the typical sources it lists.

options.text: Unobserved colonial institutions shape both democracy and growth and are left out of the model.
options.feedback: Correct: an omitted variable that drives both the outcome and the regressor ends up in the error.

options.text: The spread of the residuals is larger for countries with high growth.
options.feedback: Revisit the glossary entry on endogeneity and the typical sources it lists.

options.text: Five-century changes in log GDP per capita are measured with substantial error.
options.feedback: Correct: measurement error in the regressor is one of the sources the glossary lists.

exam.explanation: Glossary (Endogeneity): omitted variables, simultaneous causality, and measurement error make a regressor correlated with the error. Correlation among regressors (multicollinearity) and nonconstant error variance (heteroskedasticity) do not.

exam.concept: Omitted variables bias formula (Key Takeaways, Practice Exercise 1)
exam.stem: Suppose a variable omitted from the democracy regression lowers democracy (β₃ < 0) and is positively correlated with growth (δ₂₃ > 0). Using the chapter's formula Bias = β₃ × δ₂₃, how is the growth coefficient affected?

options.text: It is biased upward: it overstates the association with growth.
options.feedback: Revisit how the omitted variables bias formula combines the two signs (Key Takeaways).

options.text: It is biased downward: it understates the association with growth.
options.feedback: Correct: a negative β₃ times a positive δ₂₃ gives a negative bias.

options.text: It is unbiased, because the two opposite signs cancel each other out.
options.feedback: Revisit how the omitted variables bias formula combines the two signs (Key Takeaways).

options.text: Its bias cannot be signed without knowing the standard errors.
options.feedback: Revisit how the omitted variables bias formula combines the two signs (Key Takeaways).

exam.explanation: Key Takeaways: Bias = β₃ × δ₂₃, where β₃ is the omitted variable's effect and δ₂₃ the slope from regressing it on the included regressor. (−) × (+) is negative, so the estimate is pushed down.

exam.stem: In the base earnings regression, the education coefficient is 5,811, with a default standard error of 570 and a robust (HC1) standard error of 642. Which value is closest to the t-statistic based on the robust standard error?

options.feedback: Correct: t = 5,811/642 ≈ 9.1 (the chapter's exact value is 9.06).
Revisit how the t-statistic is formed from the coefficient and its robust standard error (Section 16.5).
Revisit how the t-statistic is formed from the coefficient and its robust standard error (Section 16.5).
Revisit how the t-statistic is formed from the coefficient and its robust standard error (Section 16.5).

exam.explanation: Section 16.5: the coefficient is unchanged under HC1; only the standard error changes. t = 5,811/642 ≈ 9.1, down from 10.2 with the default SE; education remains highly significant.

exam.concept: Comparing default and robust standard errors (Section 16.5)
exam.stem: In the base earnings regression, the default and robust standard errors are 154 and 151 for age, and 570 and 642 for education. The chapter reads this comparison as evidence of strong heteroskedasticity that makes the default standard errors badly misleading.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter interprets this standard-error comparison (Section 16.5).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The chapter calls these modest differences, suggesting mild heteroskedasticity at most (age's robust SE is even slightly smaller).

exam.explanation: Section 16.5: the robust/default ratios are about 0.98 (age) and 1.12 (education), modest differences that suggest mild heteroskedasticity at most. Robust SEs remain the safe default for cross-sectional data.

exam.stem: Which statement about heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1/White) standard errors matches Key Concept 16.4?

options.text: They are valid whether or not heteroskedasticity is present, so the chapter uses them by default for cross-sections.
options.feedback: Correct. Using them costs little when errors are homoskedastic and protects inference when they are not.

options.text: They correct the coefficient estimates for the bias that heteroskedasticity creates, which is why the estimates change.
options.feedback: Revisit what HC1 changes and what it leaves untouched (Key Concept 16.4).

options.text: They should be used only after a formal test has confirmed heteroskedasticity, since otherwise they are invalid.
options.feedback: Revisit when the chapter recommends using robust standard errors (Key Concept 16.4).

options.text: They also account for errors that are correlated over time, so time-series regressions need no further correction.
options.feedback: Revisit which kind of error structure HC1 standard errors are built for (Sections 16.5–16.6).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.4: OLS coefficients remain unbiased under heteroskedasticity, but default SEs are wrong. HC1 standard errors are valid whether or not heteroskedasticity is present, so they are the default for cross-sections; time series need HAC SEs.

exam.stem: In the chapter's simulated time series, the residuals of the regression of y1 on x have a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.80. What does this mean?

options.text: About 80% of the residuals in the simulated sample are positive rather than negative.
options.feedback: Revisit what an autocorrelation measures (Section 16.6).

options.text: A positive residual tends to be followed by another positive residual, about 0.8 times as large on average.
options.feedback: Correct. Errors cluster: positive follows positive and negative follows negative.

options.text: The residuals and the regressor x have a correlation of about 0.80 in the simulated sample.
options.feedback: Revisit what an autocorrelation measures (Section 16.6).

options.text: The residuals grow by about 80% in absolute size from one period to the next one.
options.feedback: Revisit what an autocorrelation measures (Section 16.6).

exam.explanation: Section 16.6: the lag-1 autocorrelation is the correlation between uₜ and uₜ₋₁. With ρ ≈ 0.8, if this period's error is +1, the next period's is +0.8 on average.

exam.stem: The residual autocorrelations of the simulated regression are about 0.80, 0.31, and 0.09 at lags 1, 5, and 10. Because the lag-10 value is close to zero, the errors are effectively independent, and default standard errors are adequate.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter reads this pattern of autocorrelations and what it implies for default standard errors (Section 16.6).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The large early autocorrelations decay geometrically, the signature of AR(1) errors, so default SEs understate uncertainty.

exam.explanation: Section 16.6: the residual ACF decays geometrically (0.80, then about 0.8⁵ ≈ 0.33 at lag 5), the classic signature of AR(1) errors. Significant autocorrelation at the early lags makes default standard errors too small; HAC SEs are needed.

exam.stem: The simulation has n = 10,000 observations with AR(1) errors and ρ = 0.8. Using the chapter's variance factor (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ), what is the approximate effective sample size?

options.text: About 2,000
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter turns the variance factor into an effective sample size (Section 16.6).

options.text: About 1,111
options.feedback: Correct: (1 + 0.8)/(1 − 0.8) = 9, so the effective sample size is about 10,000/9 ≈ 1,111.

options.text: About 8,000
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter turns the variance factor into an effective sample size (Section 16.6).

options.text: About 90,000
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter turns the variance factor into an effective sample size (Section 16.6).

exam.explanation: Section 16.6: with AR(1) errors, Var(ū) ≈ σ²·(1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ)·(1/n) = 9σ²/n for ρ = 0.8, so the effective sample size is about n/9 ≈ 1,111.

exam.stem: In the simulated regression of y1 on x (n = 10,000, AR(1) errors with ρ = 0.8, true slope 2), the OLS slope estimate is 2.006. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: HC1 robust standard errors solve the problem, because they are built for errors that are correlated over time.
options.feedback: Revisit which kind of error structure each type of robust standard error is built for (Sections 16.5–16.6).

options.text: OLS remains unbiased here, consistent with an estimate so close to the true slope.
options.feedback: Correct. Autocorrelation does not bias OLS; it affects the standard errors.

options.text: Default standard errors tend to understate the uncertainty in the slope.
options.feedback: Correct. Positively correlated errors carry less independent information than the default formula assumes.

options.text: HAC (Newey–West) standard errors allow for both heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation.
options.feedback: Correct. That is what makes them the chapter's remedy for time series.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.5: with autocorrelated errors, OLS is unbiased, but default SEs are typically too small, overstating significance. HAC (Newey–West) SEs account for both heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation.

exam.stem: Suppose the chapter's simulation used T = 8,000 observations instead of 10,000. What lag length L would the rule of thumb L ≈ 0.75 × T<sup>1/3</sup> give?

options.text: About 67
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's rule of thumb for the HAC lag length (Section 16.6).

options.text: About 20
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's rule of thumb for the HAC lag length (Section 16.6).

options.text: About 6,000
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's rule of thumb for the HAC lag length (Section 16.6).

options.text: About 15

exam.explanation: Section 16.6: L ≈ 0.75 × T<sup>1/3</sup> = 0.75 × 8,000<sup>1/3</sup> = 0.75 × 20 = 15 (for the chapter's T = 10,000 it gives about 16). A larger L captures more of the decaying autocorrelation but adds noise.

exam.concept: Adding controls to the democracy regression (Section 16.7)
exam.stem: Adding constraint, indcent, catholic, muslim, and protestant to the regression of democracy on growth changes the growth coefficient from 0.131 (t ≈ 6.7) to 0.047 (t ≈ 1.8, p ≈ 0.07). Which reading follows the chapter?

options.text: Part of the bivariate association reflected institutional and religious factors that are related to both democracy and growth.
options.feedback: Correct. The bivariate regression attributed some of those factors' influence to growth.

options.text: The controls created multicollinearity, which pulled the growth coefficient toward zero.
options.feedback: Revisit what multicollinearity does and does not do to OLS coefficients (Section 16.1).

options.text: The bivariate estimate is the unbiased one, since adding regressors can only add bias.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's comparison of the bivariate and multiple regressions (Section 16.7).

options.text: Growth is now shown to have no effect on democracy, since p ≈ 0.07 proves the null hypothesis.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value above 0.05 does and does not establish.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.6: the growth coefficient falls by 64% once institutional controls enter, a sign of omitted variables bias in the bivariate model. Failing to reject at 5% does not prove the effect is zero.

exam.stem: Suppose the residual-versus-fitted plot for an earnings regression shows a flat LOWESS smooth at zero, but the residuals spread out like a megaphone as fitted earnings rise. What does this indicate, and what is the chapter's response?

options.text: Autocorrelation; use HAC (Newey–West) standard errors.
options.feedback: Revisit the patterns the chapter describes for residual-versus-fitted plots (Section 16.8).

options.text: A missing nonlinear term; add a quadratic in the regressors.
options.feedback: Revisit the patterns the chapter describes for residual-versus-fitted plots (Section 16.8).

options.text: Heteroskedasticity; use robust standard errors or a log transformation.
options.feedback: Correct. A fan shape signals error variance that grows with the fitted values; the coefficients stay unbiased, but the default standard errors do not.

options.text: Influential observations; delete the points with the largest residuals first.
options.feedback: Revisit the patterns the chapter describes for residual-versus-fitted plots and its advice on influential observations (Section 16.8).

exam.explanation: Section 16.8: a fan (megaphone) shape in the residual-versus-fitted plot signals heteroskedasticity, common in income data; remedies are robust SEs, a log transformation, or WLS. A curved LOWESS would signal nonlinearity instead.

exam.stem: Which statements about the diagnostic plots for the democracy model are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A LOWESS curve that bends away from the straight line in the component-plus-residual plot for growth would suggest a nonlinear relationship with growth.
options.feedback: Correct. The component-plus-residual plot is designed to detect nonlinearity in one regressor.

options.text: In the actual-versus-fitted plot, points scattered evenly around the 45° line, with a LOWESS that follows it, indicate no systematic prediction error.
options.feedback: Correct. Deviations of the LOWESS from the 45° line would signal systematic errors.

options.text: Autocorrelation is easiest to detect in the residual-versus-fitted scatter plot.
options.feedback: Revisit which plots the chapter uses to detect each problem (Section 16.8).

options.text: Points lying close to the 45° line in the actual-versus-fitted plot would show that growth has a causal effect on democracy.
options.feedback: Revisit what diagnostic plots can and cannot establish (Section 16.8).

options.text: A LOWESS smooth is a nonparametric curve that helps reveal patterns hard to see in the raw scatter.
options.feedback: Correct. LOWESS fits a flexible local curve through the points.

exam.explanation: Section 16.8 and Key Concept 16.7: random scatter around zero is the healthy pattern; a curved LOWESS signals nonlinearity; the actual-versus-fitted LOWESS should follow the 45° line. Autocorrelation needs a time-series plot or ACF.

exam.stem: The added-variable plot for growth graphs the residuals from regressing democracy on the five controls against the residuals from regressing growth on the same controls. What does the slope of the fitted line in this plot equal?

options.text: The coefficient on growth in the bivariate regression of democracy on growth
options.feedback: Revisit what the added-variable plot purges from both variables (Key Concept 16.7).

options.text: The correlation between democracy and growth
options.feedback: Revisit what the added-variable plot purges from both variables (Key Concept 16.7).

options.text: The coefficient on growth in the regression that includes all five controls
options.feedback: Correct. Purging both variables of the controls leaves the partial relationship, whose slope is the multiple regression coefficient.

options.text: The R² of the regression that includes all five controls
options.feedback: Revisit what the added-variable plot purges from both variables (Key Concept 16.7).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.7: the added-variable plot purges both y and x<sub>j</sub> of the other regressors, so its slope equals the OLS coefficient b<sub>j</sub> from the full model (the chapter's Panel C).

exam.stem: The democracy model has k = 7 coefficients (including the intercept) and n = 131 countries. Using the chapter's rule of thumb, above what absolute value of DFITS should a country be investigated?

options.feedback: Revisit the DFITS rule of thumb (Key Concept 16.8).
Revisit the DFITS rule of thumb (Key Concept 16.8).
Revisit the DFITS rule of thumb (Key Concept 16.8).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.8: investigate if |DFITS<sub>i</sub>| > 2√(k/n) = 2√(7/131) ≈ 0.46.

exam.stem: In the democracy model, suppose one country's DFBETAS for the growth coefficient is well above the chapter's threshold, while its DFBETAS values for the other coefficients are small. What does this indicate?

options.text: The country has high leverage, since DFBETAS measures how unusual its regressor values are.
options.feedback: Revisit what DFBETAS measures (Key Concept 16.8).

options.text: The country has an unusually large residual, so it should be deleted before the model is re-estimated.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's advice on what to do with flagged observations (Section 16.8).

options.text: The growth coefficient would barely change if the country were dropped, since its other DFBETAS values are small.
options.feedback: Revisit what DFBETAS measures (Key Concept 16.8).

options.text: Dropping the country would noticeably change the growth coefficient, while barely changing the others.
options.feedback: Correct. DFBETAS is specific to each coefficient.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 16.8: DFBETAS<sub>j,i</sub> is the scaled change in b<sub>j</sub> when observation i is excluded. One country can be influential for the growth coefficient and not for the others.

exam.stem: Five of the 131 countries exceed the DFITS threshold. Following the chapter, the right response is to drop these five countries and report the estimates from the remaining 126 countries.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's advice on what to do with flagged observations (Section 16.8).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. DFITS is a screening tool: investigate the five countries, correct data errors, keep genuine cases, and check whether conclusions change without them.

exam.explanation: Section 16.8 and Key Concept 16.8: don't automatically delete influential observations, and don't report only the post-deletion results. Investigate them and report how sensitive the results are.

exam.concept: Leverage and influence (Section 16.8, Key Concepts glossary)
exam.stem: Suppose a country has a very unusual combination of regressor values (high leverage), but its democracy change lies almost exactly on the fitted regression surface (tiny residual). What does this mean?

options.text: It is likely the most influential country, since high leverage is what drives influence.
options.feedback: Revisit the glossary entries on leverage and Cook's distance (Section 16.8).

options.text: Its leverage is high because its democracy value is unusual.
options.feedback: Revisit what leverage measures (Key Concepts glossary).

options.text: It is a data error, because high-leverage points do not occur in correct data.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's discussion of genuinely unusual cases (Section 16.8).

options.text: It has the potential to move the fitted line, but because it fits the pattern, its actual influence is small.
options.feedback: Correct. Influence combines leverage with residual size; a high-leverage point that fits the pattern exerts little pull.

exam.explanation: Glossary (Leverage, Cook's Distance) and Section 16.8: leverage measures how unusual xᵢ is; influence (DFITS, Cook's distance) combines leverage with the size of the residual. Points are most influential when both are large.

exam.stem: Using the glossary's rule of thumb, above what value of Cook's distance should one of the 131 countries be investigated?

options.feedback: Revisit the glossary's rule of thumb for Cook's distance.
Revisit the glossary's rule of thumb for Cook's distance.
Revisit the glossary's rule of thumb for Cook's distance.

exam.explanation: Glossary (Cook's Distance): investigate values above 4/n = 4/131 ≈ 0.031. In the democracy model, five countries exceed it.

exam.stem: For the linear regression of earnings on age and education, Ramsey's RESET test (which adds ŷ² and ŷ³) rejects with p < 0.001. By the glossary, this points to a misspecified functional form, such as a missing nonlinear term.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Rejecting RESET signals that the linear form misses nonlinear structure.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit what the RESET test checks (Key Concepts glossary).

exam.explanation: Glossary (RESET): adding powers of the fitted values and testing them jointly checks the functional form; rejection signals a misspecified model, typically a missing nonlinear term.

exam.concept: Choosing remedies for data and model problems (Sections 16.1–16.8)
exam.stem: Which pairings of a problem and a remedy follow the chapter's guidance? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: An endogenous regressor: switch to HC1 robust standard errors
options.feedback: Revisit what problem each type of standard error addresses (Sections 16.2–16.5).

options.text: Heteroskedastic errors in a cross-section of workers: weighted least squares (WLS)
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter's table lists WLS, alongside robust SEs, for heteroskedasticity.

options.text: A measured confounder correlated with the regressor of interest: add it as a control
options.feedback: Correct: including relevant controls reduces omitted variables bias.

options.text: Severe multicollinearity between two regressors: switch to HC1 robust standard errors
options.feedback: Revisit what problem each type of standard error addresses (Sections 16.1 and 16.5).

options.text: Autocorrelated errors in a quarterly time series: feasible GLS (FGLS)
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter's table lists FGLS, alongside HAC SEs, for autocorrelation.

exam.explanation: Sections 16.2–16.7: the chapter's table pairs heteroskedasticity with robust SEs or WLS and autocorrelation with HAC SEs or FGLS; omitted confounders call for added controls. Robust SEs fix neither endogeneity bias nor the imprecision caused by multicollinearity.
